title: Independent Events and Unions of Events
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.7 Independent Events and Unions of Events
intro: After this lesson you can test whether two events are independent, use $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ only when they are, and find the probability of a union with $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.

moments.title: Independent events
moments.text: Knowing that one event occurred does not change the probability of the other.

moments.title: Conditions that show independence
moments.text: $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ or $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$. Any one of these checks is enough.

moments.title: Compare matching events
moments.text: Whatever event is in the condition on the left must be the event you compare against on the right.

moments.title: Multiplication rule for independent events
moments.text: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)$, valid only when the events are independent.

moments.title: Not independent means associated
moments.text: Being female changed the chance of ordering hot coffee, so the variables are associated.

moments.title: Union of events
moments.text: $P(A\cup B)$ is the probability of $A$ or $B$ or both.

moments.title: Addition rule
moments.text: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. The subtraction stops the overlap being counted twice.

moments.title: Neither is the complement of the union
Mixed questions on $E$ and $D$
moments.text: Mutually exclusive, union, conditional and independent checks from $P(E)=0.27$, $P(D)=0.51$, $P(E\cap D)=0.07$.

moments.title: Solve for $P(B)$
moments.text: Substitute into the addition rule. Use 0 for the joint if mutually exclusive, or $P(A)P(B)$ if independent.

cards.name: Not independent
cards.text: The conditional probability differs from the overall probability.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Independence is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent, because one occurring makes the other impossible.

sections.title: Test independence, then find a union

questions.obj: Test whether two events are independent from a table
questions.q: Of 150 customers, 63 ordered hot coffee. Of the 80 female customers, 28 ordered hot coffee. Are being female and ordering hot coffee independent?

steps.t: Find the probability of the event with no condition.

work.text: This is the baseline: 63 of the 150 customers ordered hot coffee.

steps.t: Add the condition and divide by the size of that group.

work.text: Only the 80 females count, so 80 is the denominator.

steps.t: Compare the two probabilities. Match the event before the bar with the event on the other side.

work.text: Independent events have $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Here the conditional probability is different.
Say whether knowing the condition changed the probability.

questions.answer: Being female and ordering hot coffee are not independent. The probability of ordering hot coffee is 0.42 overall but only 0.35 for females, so being female changes the probability.

questions.obj: Find the probability of a union with the addition rule
questions.q: Of 150 customers, 80 are female, 58 ordered iced coffee, and 36 are female and ordered iced coffee. Find the probability that a randomly selected customer is female or ordered iced coffee.

steps.t: Write the union event with "or" meaning one, the other, or both.

work.text: "Or" includes customers who are in both groups.
The 36 customers who are both were counted in each of the two totals.

steps.t: Subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice.

work.text: The overlap deserves to be counted once, not twice.
Fifty-eight iced coffee drinkers and 80 females, less the 36 who are both, gives 102 customers.

questions.answer: The probability that a randomly selected customer is female or ordered iced coffee is 0.68.

questions.obj: Solve for a missing probability when the events are independent
questions.q: $P(A)=0.25$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.62$. The events $A$ and $B$ are independent. Find $P(B)$.

work.text: The rule links the three probabilities you are given or asked for.

steps.t: Let $x=P(B)$ and use independence to replace the joint probability.

work.text: Multiplying is allowed because the problem says the events are independent.
Subtract 0.25 from both sides, then divide by 0.75.

traps.title: Justify non-independence with two numbers
traps.weak: Science and math are not independent.
traps.better: $P(\text{science})=0.25$ but $P(\text{science}\mid\text{math})=0.12/0.30=0.40$. The probabilities differ, so the events are not independent.

traps.title: Multiplying without independence
traps.better: Multiplication is allowed only when the events are independent. Otherwise use $P(A)\,P(B\mid A)$.

traps.title: Forgetting to subtract the overlap
traps.better: 36 customers are counted twice. Subtract the overlap: $(80+58-36)/150=0.68$.

traps.title: Mutually exclusive confused with independent
traps.weak: The events are mutually exclusive, so they are independent.
traps.better: If $P(A\cap B)=0$ and both probabilities are positive, then $P(A\cap B)\ne P(A)P(B)$, so the events are not independent.

traps.title: Mismatched comparison
traps.better: Compare $P(A\mid B)$ to $P(A)$, or $P(B\mid A)$ to $P(B)$. The event before the bar must match the event on the other side.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A)=0.5$ and $P(B)=0.2$. What is $P(A\cup B)$?
why: This adds the probabilities without subtracting the overlap.
Subtracting the probabilities is not a rule for the union.

questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A)=0.40$, $P(B)=0.30$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.12$. Which statement is correct?
opts: $A$ and $B$ are not independent because $P(A\mid B)\ne P(A)$.
why: The conditional probability equals $P(A)$, so the events are independent.

questions.stem: If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, $P(A)=0.30$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.55$, what is $P(B)$?
why: This does not use the addition rule.

questions.stem: In a school, 40% of students play a sport and 30% are in a club. 12% do both. What is the probability a student plays a sport or is in a club?
why: This is the probability of doing both.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A survey of 200 students asked whether they take Spanish and whether they play in the school band. The counts were: both 30, Spanish only 50, band only 45, neither 75.
parts: (a) Find the probability that a randomly selected student takes Spanish or plays in the band.
(c) Are taking Spanish and playing in the band independent? Justify.
(d) Another pair of events $E$ and $F$ has $P(E)=0.40$, $P(F)=0.25$ and $P(E\cup F)=0.55$. Find $P(E\cap F)$.
sample: (c) Yes. $P(\text{Spanish})=80/200=0.40$ and $P(\text{Spanish}\mid\text{band})=0.40$. The probabilities are equal, so the events are independent.
